full_judgment:
2. The facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule are that the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1, Md Nurul Islam, instituted the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2004 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Charfasion, Bhola for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 stating, inter alia, that the case land appertaining to SA Plot No. 52 and 278 under SA Khatian No. 12 belonged to Ashini Kumar and others. Aswini Kumar sold out some portion of land to Ayesha Khatun. Aswini Kumar further sold out 4 anna 11 gonda 3 kora share to Chandra Kumar Mazi who died leaving behind his 2 (two) sons, Manik Chandra Mazi and Khagandra Chandra Mazi who sold out 61 decimals of land by a registered deed dated 27-3-2003 to the pre-emptor. Haripad Mazi, son of Ashini Kumar Mazi sold out 1.22 acres of land to the pre-emptor by a registered deed dated 9-5-1996. As such, the pre-emptor became co-sharer, owner and possessor of 1.83 acres of land in the disputed Khatian described in the schedule of the pre-emption case. The opposite party No. 2, Abdul Zabbar is one of the co-sharers of the holding who sold out 64 decimals of land on 3-4-2004 to the pre-emptee No. 1, Md Soleman who is the stranger to the case holding without giving any notice to other co-sharers including the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor obtained certified copy on 13-6-2004 of the sale deed and came to know properly as to the transfer of sale and filed the Pre-emption Case No. 27 of 2004. 

 5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Charfashion, Bhola, the pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 12 of 2011 in the Court of District Judge, Bhola which was transferred to the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Bhola. On hearing both the sides, the learned Joint District Judge allowed the miscellaneous appeal on 11-7-2012 allowing the pre-emption reversing the judgment and order dated 23-2-2011 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge on the ground that the pre-emptee Md Soleman did not state clearly on what date, time and place and in whose presence the proposal to sell the property was given to the pre-emptor and it cannot be considered by the simple word that proposal was given to him which was refused by him. He also decided that the pre-emption case is not barred by the doctrine of waiver and acquiescence, limitation and defect of parties. 

 8. Mr Md Shahadat Hossen Palash, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1, submits that the learned Senior Assistant Judge wrongly disallowed the pre-emption case on the ground of waiver and acquiescence but he did not state a single sentence in the judgment as to waiver, acquiescence and estoppel. Moreover, he submits that this pre-emption case was not barred by doctrine of waiver, acquiescence and estoppel and even there is no defect of party. 

 11. The main question in this case is to be decided whether the pre-emption case is barred by the doctrine of waiver, acquiescence and estoppel. It appears from the materials on record that the purchaser Md Soleman did not state in his written objection and deposition on what date, time and place and in what manner, in whose presence offer to sell was given to the pre-emptor and he proposed to purchase the land by giving Taka 40,000 which was less than the present market value. 

 12. On careful scrutiny of the record, it appears that there is no evidence on record from which it can be decided that the pre-emption case is barred by doctrine of waiver, acquiescence and estoppel. There is no material on record to show that the pre-emptor took any part in bargaining about the transaction or assisting in any way the seller in selling the land or induces the buyer to make the purchase or that the pre-emptor negotiated the said sale. In fact, the pre-emptee No. 1 failed to prove that the pre-emptor has waived or abandoned his statutory right of pre-emption. Although the learned Assistant Judge framed an issue as to whether the pre-emptor-petitioner was aware of the sale or not, but he did not state a single line regarding this issue. The learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Charfashion, Bhola rightly and legally decided in appeal that the respondent did not clearly state on what date, time, place, in what manner and in whose presence the offer of sale was refused by the pre-emptor. He also rightly decided that by the simple statement made in the written objection as to refusal of purchasing the case land cannot be considered that the pre-emptor waived the right of pre-emption. Moreover, on perusal of the record, it appears that there is no evidence on record as to what kind of role was played by the pre-emptor during the sale and purchase process for which it can be decided that the case is barred by the principle of waiver, acquiescence and estoppel. 

 13. The learned Advocate for the pre-emptor-opposite party relied upon the decisions, passed by the Hon'ble lordships reported in 15 MLR (AD) 128 and 1994 BLD (AD) 29 = 44 DLR (AD) 62, are very much relevant in the instant case. It appears from the case of Md Abdur Rahim vs Md Amirul Islam and others reported in 15 MLR (AD) 128 that the pre-emptor filed a Miscellaneous Pre-emption Case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the first Court of Rajshahi claiming pre-emption of the case land. In that case the pre-emptee-purchaser raised the question that the preemption case is barred by the principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence but the Hon'ble High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record came to the definite findings that the pre-emption proceeding was not barred by the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The Hon'ble Appellate Division, in that case, decided that there was also no materials on record to show that the pre-emptor took part in bringing about the transaction or assisted in any way the sellers in selling the land or induced the buyers to make the purchase or that the pre-emptor negotiated the price of the case land. 

 14. It also appears from the case of Fazaruddin vs Maijuddin and others reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 29 = 44 DLR (AD) 62 that the co-sharers Mariam and Alimunnessa sold out their paternal property to the stranger-respondents without serving notice to the pre-emptor-petitioner who is a co-sharer to the holding by two separate registered sale deeds dated 9-5-1973 and 10-5-1973. The pre-emptor petitioner filed two separate pre-emption cases under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the 1st court of Munsif, Dhaka. In that case question as to waiver and acquiescence was raised on the ground that the OPW 1 has testified that the pre-emptor had even given assurance that he would not claim pre-emption. The Hon'ble Appellate division held that the right of pre-emption accrues after transfer of the land, and statutory right of pre-emption cannot be taken away by mere verbal assurance of the person, having such right unless clearly make out a case of acquiescence or waiver. On perusal of the materials on record I am of the view that purchaser-opposite party failed to make out a case of acquiescence, waiver and estoppel. 

 15. In the light of the decisions passed by the Hon'ble Apex Court and discussions made above I am of the view that the learned Joint District Judge rightly stated in his judgment that there is no waiver, acquiescence and estoppel in the instant case. The grounds stated by the learned Senior Assistant Judge rejecting the pre-emption petition in his judgment are not lawful and well reasoned.
